newsitem.title: USA: Motorola installs cable Internet access.
newsitem.headline: Motorola installs cable Internet access.

text.p: Motorola Inc said Tuesday it was in the process of setting up cable Internet access infrastructure in at least four cities and has already sold about 500,000 cable modems for these services.

On Tuesday, Time Warner Inc launched its high-speed online service which operates over cable networks in Akron and Canton, Ohio. Motorola installed the infrastructure and is the primary vendor of modems. For this service alone it sold 50,000 of its CyberSURFR modems.

"We have our teams installing systems in four or five (other) cities, just with Time Warner," said Jim Phillips, corporate vice president of Motorola's multimedia group, in a telephone interview from the service launch in Akron.
He said in addition to Time Warner, Motorola is working with TCI Communications Inc, At Home Corp and Comcast Corp to set up cable Internet access.

"We also received over half a million (orders for modems) from a variety of cable and Bell operating companies here in the United States," Phillips said. "Half a million already and here's our first launch, so it's a good business."

With the modem and infrastructure, Internet access is much faster over upgraded cable television networks than over the traditional telephone lines. Technology such as ADSL (asymmetrical digital subscriber line), however, is also being implemented to add speed to telephone line access.

Motorola installs the cable routers, Phillips said, and provides the modems that hook up the cable to personal computers. The cable companies buy the modems and give them to subscribers, much like cable TV set-top boxes.

Securities analysts said Motorola is a key player in the cable Internet access market, and sales of the modems and infrastructure may even have an impact on the company's earnings within the next year.

"Cable modems are hot products, and we'll have to see how fast the infrastructure can be upgraded to make this into a big market, but Motorola is exceptionally well positioned," said Matt Robison, an analyst for Montgomery Securities. "A few quarters out it may be recognizable in Motorola's numbers."
Nonetheless, the cable companies first must upgrade the networks for two-way traffic. At this point most are only able to broadcast from one point to many homes.
"There is an enormous amount of work that has to be done before the cable modem will be big," said one analyst, who asked not to be named. "The cable network is just not in shape."
